Client: Sure, just last week, I missed a minor deadline. Immediately, I started thinking, “This is it, they're going to fire me.” It was overwhelming.
Counselor: Thank you for sharing that example. Let's examine that thought a bit. What evidence do you have that missing this deadline will lead to you being fired?
Client: Well, I can't say there's direct evidence, but it's this constant fear that I'm not doing enough or meeting expectations.
Counselor: I see. On the other hand, what evidence might suggest that missing one deadline isn't catastrophic?
Client: Well, I guess I've missed small deadlines before and didn't get fired. My boss didn't explicitly say my job was at risk either.
Counselor: That's a good observation. It seems like there's a pattern where your mind quickly jumps to the worst-case scenario. How do you think it would feel to consider alternative outcomes when these situations arise?
Client: I guess it would feel less intense, less panicky. But it's tough to think that way when I'm in the moment.
Counselor: Understandably so. What we can work on together is creating alternative thoughts that you can turn to when your anxiety spikes. For example, what could be a more balanced thought you might have had about missing last week's deadline?
Client: Maybe something like, “It was just one deadline, and I've done well in other areas”?
Counselor:
output: That's a good start. We can practice this reframe and see how it influences your feelings over time. Also, we might conduct some experiments where you try making small changes to your work hours and we observe the outcomes. How does that sound?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Megan. I'm glad you're here today. What brings you to counseling?
Client: Hi. I've been feeling pretty low lately about not being married. I keep thinking that it's probably because of my negative attitude, and maybe that's why no one wants to be with me.
Counselor: That sounds really tough, Megan. When did you start noticing these feelings about your relationship status?
Client: It started a few years ago when many of my friends began getting married. Ever since then, I've constantly been comparing myself to them and feeling more and more pressured.
Counselor: It seems like this comparison and societal pressure have been adding to your stress. What kind of thoughts come to mind when you see happy couples or attend relationship-focused social events?
Client: I usually think that there's something wrong with me, that my bad attitude is the reason I'm still single. It's like I can't help but believe that people wouldn't want to be with me because of it.
Counselor: Those thoughts must be really challenging to deal with. You mentioned trying positive thinking and self-reflection. How did that go for you?
Client: Not very well, to be honest. I just keep ending up with the same negative thoughts. It feels like no matter how much I try to think positively, that negative self-talk keeps winning.
Counselor: It sounds like this negative self-talk is quite persistent. How has this impacted other areas of your life, like your job performance or relationships with friends?
Client: I've noticed that my job performance has suffered a bit. It's hard to focus when I'm constantly doubting myself. And with my friends, I feel like I'm always criticizing myself, which has put some strain on our relationships.
Counselor: It's understandable that constant self-criticism would have such effects. Do you usually find time to talk to your friends about what you're going through?
Client: Not really. I have a supportive group of friends, but I haven't shared these specific thoughts with them. I don't want to burden them with my problems.
Counselor: It can be tough to open up about such personal thoughts. Given how you've been feeling, what would you like to get out of our sessions together?
Client: I just want to stop feeling so negative about myself and my situation. I want to be able to see things differently and not let these thoughts control my life so much.
Counselor: That's a valuable goal. Let's start by looking at some of these negative thoughts. Can you give an example of a specific thought or situation that triggers these feelings?
Client: Sure. When I attended a friend's wedding recently, I couldn't help but think, "I'll never find someone for myself because I'm just too negative and unlovable."
Counselor: That's an intense thought to have at such an event. What do you think when you hear yourself saying that?
Client: It feels pretty harsh, but I can't seem to shake it off. It's like a constant reminder in my head.
Counselor: It sounds quite powerful. Let's consider for a moment if there might be any other way of looking at that situation. Is there any evidence that might contradict the idea that you are unlovable or too negative?
Client: Well, my friends do say I'm fun to be around and smart. But then I wonder if they're just saying that to make me feel better.
Counselor: It sounds like there's a part of you that can recognize some of your strengths, even if it's hard to fully believe them right now. What might happen if you started focusing more on these positive attributes?
Client: Maybe I'd feel better about myself, but it's hard to keep that focus when the negative thoughts are so loud.
Counselor: It can be a challenge to shift focus, especially when those negative thoughts have been there for a while. One thing that might help is practicing self-compassion and being kinder to yourself. How does the idea of self-compassion feel to you?
Client: It sounds nice, but honestly, I struggle with it. I feel like I don't deserve to be kind to myself.
Counselor: It's common to feel that way, especially when you're used to criticizing yourself. But everyone deserves kindness, including you. What do you think might change if you started treating yourself with the same compassion you show your friends?
Client: I guess I'd be a lot less stressed and maybe feel more at peace with my situation.
Counselor:
output: That sounds like a positive change. As we work through your thoughts and perceptions, self-compassion can be a helpful tool. How about we explore some exercises you can try between our sessions to practice reframing those thoughts with more positive perspectives?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi Greg, I'm glad you're here today. How can I be of assistance?
Client: Hi. I've been feeling pretty guilty and afraid lately, especially when it comes to my grandchildren. I just feel like I'm letting them down.
Counselor: That sounds really tough. Can you tell me more about when these feelings started and what might have triggered them?
Client: Well, it began when I became a grandparent at a relatively young age, 44. Since then, balancing work and family has become more stressful, and these feelings intensified recently.
Counselor: It sounds like you have a lot on your plate. How have these feelings impacted your daily life?
Client: They've made it harder to focus at work and to enjoy spending time with my grandkids. I constantly worry I'm not meeting their expectations.
Counselor: That constant worry must be exhausting. Have you noticed any particular times when these feelings are stronger?
Client: Mostly after long days at work or when I have to be away from my grandchildren. I just feel that I'm not doing enough for them.
Counselor: It seems like these feelings are significantly affecting your well-being. Have you tried anything to manage these feelings?
Client: Yes, I've tried to spend more quality time with my grandchildren and do activities I enjoy, but it doesn't seem to help much.
Counselor: It sounds like you're making an effort, which is commendable. What activities do you enjoy doing with your grandchildren?
Client: We enjoy playing games and going to the park. Those moments are good, but the guilt creeps back afterward.
Counselor: It's important to acknowledge those good moments. Let's explore what thoughts are going through your mind when the guilt resurfaces. Can you share a recent example?
Client: After a great day at the park, I thought about how I missed a few of their school events due to work and felt like a failure.
Counselor: It seems like you're focusing on the missed events rather than the positive experiences. What evidence do you have that missing those events means you're letting them down?
Client: Well, I suppose I don't. It's just a feeling that they might be disappointed in me.
Counselor: I understand. How do your grandchildren behave towards you when you spend time together?
Client: They seem happy and excited to be with me. They never say anything negative about my absence.
Counselor: That's an important observation. Their actions suggest they value your presence. Do you think it's possible you're being harder on yourself than necessary?
Client: Maybe, but it's hard not to feel responsible. I want to be there for them completely, you know?
Counselor: Absolutely, wanting to be there for them shows how much you care. How do you think you could balance your responsibilities with your desire to be present more effectively?
Client: I'm not sure. Maybe I need to find a better way to manage my time and set more realistic expectations for myself.
Counselor: That sounds like a practical approach. Would setting specific times for family activities and work be something you're open to trying?
Client: It might help, but it's difficult with my unpredictable work schedule.
Counselor: I understand. Flexibility can be challenging, but small, consistent steps towards setting boundaries may make a difference. How would you feel about exploring some strategies together?
Client: I'm willing to try. I just want to feel more at peace and present with them.
Counselor:
output: That's a good starting point. Let's work on identifying one or two strategies today and gradually build on them. What do you think might be a small, manageable change you could implement this week?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi Kevin, welcome to our session today. How are you feeling about starting this journey together?
Client: Hi, I'm a bit nervous but I'm ready to work on this. I really want to get better at making eye contact and being comfortable in social situations.
Counselor: It's great to hear that you're ready to work on this. Can you tell me a little more about when you first noticed that you had difficulty making eye contact?
Client: I think it started when I was a teenager. I had some embarrassing moments in school, and since then, I've had a hard time looking people in the eye when I talk to them.
Counselor: That sounds tough. Those past experiences seem to be affecting you even now. Can you give me an example of one of those moments, if you're comfortable sharing?
Client: Sure. There was a time when I tripped and fell in front of my classmates during a presentation. Everyone laughed, and I felt so humiliated. Since then, I just avoid eye contact because I'm scared of being judged or laughed at again.
Counselor: I understand. It's natural to want to avoid situations that make us feel uncomfortable or judged. Have there been times recently when you've found it particularly difficult to make eye contact?
Client: Yes, especially in group settings with my friends. I feel like my friends think I'm weird because I can't look them in the eye. I always imagine they're judging me or only hanging out with me out of pity.
Counselor: It's clear that these thoughts are affecting how you feel about your friendships. Let's explore this a bit more. How do you feel when you're around your friends, aside from the worry about eye contact?
Client: I actually enjoy their company a lot. They make me laugh and feel good, but the anxiety about eye contact is always in the back of my mind, making it hard to fully relax and be myself.
Counselor: It sounds like you value your friendships and have positive experiences with your friends. How do you usually respond in social gatherings when the anxiety about eye contact arises?
Client: I usually look away or down at my feet. Sometimes I pretend to check my phone just to avoid making eye contact. It's frustrating because I know it's noticeable.
Counselor: That must be really challenging for you. It seems like the anxiety is preventing you from fully engaging in social interactions. How do you feel about trying some role-playing exercises to practice making eye contact in a safe space?
Client: I'm willing to give it a try. I'm a bit nervous about the idea, but I know I need to do something different to get better.
Counselor: It's perfectly okay to feel nervous. We'll take things at your own pace. To start, let's create a simple role-playing scenario. Imagine you're talking to a friend about a movie you recently watched. How do you think you would feel doing that here?
Client: I think it would be less intimidating here than in real life situations. I could give it a shot.
Counselor: Great. Let's start easy. I'll be your friend, and we'll talk about a movie. Remember, there's no right or wrong way to do this. Just focus on making eye contact when you're comfortable. How does that sound?
Client: That sounds good to me. Okay, so I watched this action movie last weekend...
Counselor: Wonderful. As you describe the movie, try to maintain eye contact when you feel ready. Take your time.
Client: Well, it was really exciting. There were a lot of cool stunts and special effects. I couldn't look away from the screen.
Counselor: That sounds like an interesting movie. Can you tell me more about your favorite scene?
Client: The best part was the car chase through the city. The camera work was amazing, and the actors did a great job.
Counselor: It sounds like that scene really captivated you. How did you feel sharing that with me and making some eye contact?
Client: It felt a bit strange at first, but it wasn't as bad as I expected. I think I could get used to it with more practice.
Counselor: That's a positive step forward, Kevin. Practicing in a supportive environment can help you build confidence. How do you feel about doing more of these exercises in future sessions?
Client: I feel optimistic about it. I think it will help me become more comfortable with eye contact over time.
Counselor:
output: Excellent. We'll continue to incorporate these exercises and work on reframing any negative thoughts you have about social interactions. Together, we'll make gradual progress. Does that sound good?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Good morning, Ruth. It's nice to meet you. How are you feeling today?
Client: Hi. I'm here, I guess. Not great, but I'm managing.
Counselor: Thank you for sharing that. Could you tell me a bit about what's been on your mind lately?
Client: Well, I've been feeling really down about myself. It just feels like no matter what I do, people see me as a loser who will never amount to anything.
Counselor: That sounds incredibly tough, Ruth. Can you think of any specific situations where you've felt this way recently?
Client: Yeah, like when I'm out skateboarding and some people give me weird looks, or when I try to talk to someone and they don't seem interested. It's like they can see right through me.
Counselor: It must be hard to experience those reactions. When you have these thoughts, what kind of things do you usually tell yourself?
Client: I usually think about how they're right. I must be a weirdo or a slacker, just like people said when I was a teenager. It's been the same story all my life.
Counselor: It seems like those past labels are still affecting you today. How do these thoughts impact your motivation and feelings about yourself?
Client: They make me feel worthless and unmotivated. What's the point of trying if I'm just going to fail or be judged anyway?
Counselor: I can see how those thoughts could be overwhelming. Have you noticed any particular patterns or triggers that tend to bring these feelings on?
Client: Social situations are definitely a trigger. I feel so out of place and anxious, like everyone's scrutinizing my every move.
Counselor: Social situations can indeed be challenging, especially when you feel judged. When these thoughts arise, do you find yourself reacting in certain ways?
Client: Yeah, I tend to just shut down or avoid those situations altogether. It's easier than dealing with the discomfort.
Counselor: Avoidance can sometimes feel like a way to protect yourself, but it can also reinforce those negative feelings. Have you ever tried to counter these thoughts with any specific strategies?
Client: I've tried positive thinking and self-affirmations, like telling myself "I'm good at what I do" or "I matter," but they just feel empty and don't stick.
Counselor: It's understandable that these affirmations feel disconnected from your current experience. Instead, let's start by exploring the accuracy of the negative labels. Can you recall a recent instance where you felt judged and the specific thoughts you had?
Client: Just last week, a guy at the skatepark gave me this look, like he thought I didn't belong there. I immediately thought, "He thinks I'm a loser."
Counselor: That must have been very disheartening. When you had that thought, was there any evidence to support or contradict it?
Client: Well, he didn't say anything, and a few other people at the park seemed friendly enough, so maybe it was just in my head.
Counselor: It's possible that his look wasn't a judgment at all. What might be an alternative explanation for his expression?
Client: I guess he could have just been lost in his own thoughts or not actually paying attention to me. Maybe it wasn't about me at all.
Counselor: That's a good observation, Ruth. Sometimes our interpretations of others' actions can be skewed by our own fears and insecurities. How does considering this alternative perspective make you feel?
Client: A bit relieved, but also skeptical. It's hard to believe that not everyone is judging me.
Counselor: Change takes time and multiple perspectives. We'll keep working on identifying and challenging these thoughts. Can you think of a small, realistic goal you'd like to work towards in social situations?
Client: Maybe just trying to stay in the moment and not jump to conclusions so quickly. It's not much, but it's a start.
Counselor:
output: That sounds like a constructive and achievable goal. We can explore ways to practice staying present and observing without judgment. How does that sound to you?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi Grace, I'm glad you're here today. How are you feeling right now as we start our session?
Client: Hi, I'm feeling a bit down to be honest. It's been a rough few days.
Counselor: I'm sorry to hear that. Can you tell me what specifically has been on your mind?
Client: I recently went on a date that I thought went really well, but the person hasn't responded to my calls or texts since then. It's really made me feel like I'll always be alone.
Counselor: That sounds like a very tough situation. It must be difficult to deal with those feelings of loneliness and uncertainty. Can you tell me more about how this situation has been affecting you?
Client: It's been making me feel more isolated. I keep thinking that if one person doesn't want to be with me, then nobody will. It's like a constant worry now.
Counselor: It sounds like this experience has been really painful for you. When these thoughts about being alone come up, what kind of emotions do you notice yourself feeling?
Client: Mostly sadness and despair. Sometimes it makes me anxious too, like I'm worried about my future.
Counselor: Those are very strong emotions. It makes sense that they would be overwhelming. When you think about these feelings, what do you find yourself believing about your situation?
Client: I just keep thinking that this is how it's always going to be, that I'll always be rejected and alone. It feels like a certainty to me right now.
Counselor: I hear what you're saying, Grace. It's important to recognize how deeply these thoughts are affecting you. Let's take a step back for a moment. Can you think of any times in your life when things didn't turn out as badly as you feared they might?
Client: Well, I guess there have been a few times. Like when I was worried about not making any friends in college, but I did end up making some good ones. But this feels different, you know?
Counselor: It's understandable that this feels different. Each situation can carry its own weight and unique challenges. However, it's useful to see if past experiences can offer any perspective. When you think about those worries in college and how they turned out differently than you expected, what does that tell you?
Client: I suppose it tells me that sometimes my fears are worse than the actual outcome. But it's hard to see that right now when I'm feeling so low.
Counselor: It makes sense that it would be hard to see that in the midst of strong emotions. Those feelings can be very convincing and make it difficult to see other possibilities. Do you think there could be other ways to interpret your current situation?
Client: Maybe. I mean, logically I know that one date doesn't define my entire future, but it just feels so personal right now.
Counselor: It sounds like you're aware of the logical side, even if it's hard to fully believe in the moment. It's great that you're acknowledging that. What are some reasons you think this person might not have responded that aren't about you personally?
Client: I guess they could be busy, or maybe they weren't interested but didn't know how to say it. I know there are all kinds of reasons, but it still feels like a reflection on me.
Counselor: It's very common to feel that way. It's important to recognize that not hearing back can trigger self-doubt and personal feelings, even when the reasons might not have to do with you at all. What do you think might help you feel better connected with your friends or distract yourself from these thoughts?
Client: I've tried hanging out with friends and staying busy, but the loneliness still creeps in. It's like no matter what I do, the feeling is still there.
Counselor: It sounds like these feelings of loneliness are quite persistent. What are some activities you typically enjoy or feel good doing, even if just a little bit?
Client: I guess I like reading and going to the gym, though I haven't had much motivation to do those lately. 
Counselor: Finding motivation can be tough when you're feeling this way. Sometimes taking small steps towards activities you enjoy can help, even if it's just a little at a time. Have you had any moments recently where you felt even slightly better or more connected?
Client: There were a few moments when I was with friends that I felt okay, but as soon as I was alone again, the feeling came back.
Counselor: It's understandable that being alone can amplify those feelings of loneliness. Identifying and nurturing those positive moments when you're with friends can be a useful start. What's one small step you might be willing to try in the next few days to reconnect with something you enjoy?
Client: Maybe I could try going to the gym again. Even if it's just for a short workout, it might help me feel a bit better.
Counselor:
output: That sounds like a good start. Committing to even a brief activity can make a difference in how you feel. It can be helpful to acknowledge the effort you're putting in, even if it feels small. How does that plan sound to you?
patterns: black-and-white or polarized thinking / all or nothing thinking

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi Joshua, welcome. How are you feeling today?
Client: Hi, thank you. I'm a bit anxious, to be honest. I've been struggling with being late to my classes, and it's been affecting my grades and overall performance.
Counselor: I understand. It's great that you're reaching out for support. Can you tell me more about what's been happening with your punctuality and how it's impacting you?
Client: Well, it started this semester. No matter what I do, I just can't seem to get to class on time. It's led to lower grades and now it feels like everything is spiraling out of control.
Counselor: That sounds really challenging. Do you have any specific thoughts or feelings that come up when you're running late for class?
Client: Yes, I often think that I'm going to fail the entire semester because of it. It's frustrating because I feel like I'm already destined to mess things up, no matter what I try.
Counselor: It must be overwhelming to have those thoughts. Have you noticed what typically triggers these thoughts and feelings for you?
Client: Usually, it starts when I realize I'm behind schedule or when I'm rushing to get out of the house. Also, whenever I get a bad grade, it reinforces those negative thoughts.
Counselor: That makes sense—feeling behind can certainly trigger a lot of stress. Let's explore this further. When you think about being late, what do you believe will happen as a result?
Client: I believe that being late means I'll miss important parts of the lecture, fall even further behind, and eventually fail the course.
Counselor: I see. It sounds like you have some catastrophic thoughts about the outcomes of being late. How do these thoughts influence your mood and behavior?
Client: They make me incredibly anxious. Sometimes I can't even sleep at night because I'm worried about everything going downhill. It makes it even harder to wake up on time the next day.
Counselor: It's understandable that these thoughts are amplifying your anxiety. What strategies have you already tried to address your punctuality?
Client: I've set multiple alarms, made schedules, and even tried going to bed earlier. But when I wake up late, it all seems pointless and the negative thoughts just come back.
Counselor: It sounds like you've put in a lot of effort. Sometimes figuring out the underlying issues behind these patterns can make a big difference. How do you think these thoughts about inevitability contribute to your lateness?
Client: I suppose they make me feel defeated before I even begin. If I already believe I'm going to fail, I guess it affects my motivation and energy to stick to my schedule.
Counselor: That's an insightful observation. What if we were to test some of these beliefs by conducting small behavioral experiments? Collecting data on what actually happens might give you a new perspective.
Client: That sounds interesting. What kind of experiments are you thinking about?
Counselor: We might start by tracking your timeliness and what you notice when you make adjustments to your schedule. Also, recording your thoughts and feelings can help us see patterns and triggers more clearly. How does that sound?
Client: It sounds like a good plan. I've never thought of actually tracking my behaviors and thoughts systematically before.
Counselor: Great, so let's give it a try. As a start, let's set a specific goal for the next couple of days. How about trying to get to bed by a set time and noting how you feel and what thoughts you have when waking up?
Client: I can try that. I'll set a bedtime and write down my thoughts and feelings each morning.
Counselor: Excellent. During this period, also make a note of any time you're late to class and what specific thoughts you have at that moment. This will help us in understanding your thought patterns better.
Client: Okay, I'll keep track of my thoughts and feelings throughout the day, especially if I'm late.
Counselor: That sounds like a solid plan. We'll review your notes in our next session and see what patterns we can identify. How do you feel about this approach?
Client: I feel hopeful. Maybe understanding these patterns will help me manage my time better and reduce the negative thoughts.
Counselor:
output: I'm glad to hear that. Remember, this is a process and it might take some time to see changes. But each small step is progress. Is there anything else on your mind you'd like to discuss today?
patterns: black-and-white or polarized thinking / all or nothing thinking
